title: Soil structure

definition.text: The arrangement of a soil's solid particles and of the pore spaces left between them.

facts.text: Structure depends on how individual particles clump, bind and aggregate, and that in turn sets the pattern of pores between them.
It shapes water and air movement, heat conduction, biological activity, root growth, seedling emergence and resistance to erosion.
Texture is an innate property fixed by the mineral particles, but structure can be improved or destroyed by the choice and timing of farming practices.
Structure is dynamic, changing with tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and fauna, rainfall, wind erosion, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing.
Most cultivation degrades structure: mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay and oxidation.
Continued cultivation and traffic can create compacted, impermeable layers, or hardpans, within the soil profile.
Under irrigation, structure declines as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting, especially in sodic soils, where sodium makes wet particles repel one another.
Structure offers clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biological activity, history, human use and the chemical and mineral conditions under which it formed.

notes: Dossier definition line (S:99509125296f) frames structure as a geotechnical term; the Overview sentence S:85a94d8b08d0 gives the same definition without that framing.

title: Soil structure types

definition.text: The grouping of soil structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds, with five major classes: platy, prismatic, columnar, blocky and granular.

facts.text: Platy units are flat, usually horizontal plates, found mainly in subsoil compacted by trampling or machinery; they hinder the downward movement of water and roots.
Prismatic units are vertically elongated with flat to rounded vertical faces and flat tops; they typify clay-illuviated B horizons, cracked apart by freeze-thaw and wetting-drying cycles.
Columnar units resemble prisms but have distinct, rounded tops; common in subsoils of sodium-affected and swelling-clay soils, they are so dense that roots struggle to penetrate.
Blocky units are roughly equidimensional polyhedra, called angular when faces meet at sharp angles and subangular when corners are mostly rounded; they are common in subsoils and clay-rich topsoils.
Granular or crumb units are near-spherical with irregular faces not moulded on neighbouring peds; they dominate organic-rich grassland and garden topsoils and give good porosity.
Wedge units are interlocking elliptical lenses often bounded by slickensides; lenticular units are overlapping lenses parallel to the surface, linked to moist, silty soils prone to frost action.
Size classes depend on the type: very coarse means over 10 mm for platy and granular peds, over 50 mm for blocky and over 100 mm for prismlike peds.

notes: Physical properties of soil#Structure (chunk 04) also lists types, size classes and grades; merge if that pass drafts a structure-classes entry.

definition.text: A natural aggregate of soil particles, formed by soil-forming processes and separated from neighbouring units by pores or voids.

facts.text: The term is mostly used for visible structural units larger than 1 mm seen when soils are examined in the field.
A mass of soil made artificially, for example by cultivation, is a clod rather than a ped.
Clumping of sand, silt and clay into aggregates, and of aggregates into larger units, creates peds; the word is a contraction of pedolith.
Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus make soil separates adhere into these larger, relatively stable secondary structures.
Peds are best described when the soil is dry or slightly moist, because they are hard to tell apart when wet.
A soil may be structureless, have simple units with no smaller components, or have compound units built of smaller ones separated by persistent planes of weakness.
Aggregation of particles into peds is one way soil macropores form, alongside roots, cracks and soil fauna.

title: Soil aggregate stability

definition.text: A measure of how well soil aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage.

facts.text: It measures soil structure, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties.
Aggregate stability directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement.
Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while meso- and macropores let water and air move in.
Soils with good aggregate stability usually take in water faster and are not prone to ponding.
In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients.
Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors; reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs have been shown to improve aggregation.
Heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower aggregate stability.

notes: Reduced/zero tillage improves aggregation here (S:7177c78b7e07), but Soil structure#Improvement says irrigated no-till/minimum-till horticulture usually loses structure over time (S:06384642dce8).

title: Soil aggregation
article: Soil aggregate stability#Factors Affecting Aggregate Formation

definition.text: The joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation.

facts.text: Flocculated clumps become aggregates once cemented by agents such as carbonates, gypsum, sesquioxides, clay particles and organic matter.

Aggregation is strengthened by precipitated oxides and carbonates, biofilms and fungal hyphae, multivalent cations bridging negative particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds.
Calcium bridges clay and organic matter and can replace sodium on exchange sites, reducing the dispersion, crusting and slaking of sodic soils.
Iron and aluminium sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, an effect that becomes more pronounced in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides.
With 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, organic matter is the main binder; with oxides and 1:1 clays such as kaolinite, electrostatic bonds also act and aggregation is weaker.
Wetting-drying and shrink-swell cycles rearrange particles, with wetting and drying able to raise or lower stability; freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones.
Some shrink-swell soils self-mulch, forming a granular surface structure through repeated shrinking and swelling.
Earthworm casts, mite and collembola fecal pellets, roots and fungal hyphae build aggregates; such biological agents matter most in soils lacking swelling 2:1 clays.

notes: Borderline contested: S:1c7db1c448da calls wetting-drying results contradictory and offers an equilibrium hypothesis; left false because no source calls it debated.

title: Flocculation

definition.text: The drawing together of primary soil particles by inter-particle forces into microscopic clumps called floccules.

facts.text: The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding.
It is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart; the balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content.
Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates; sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay.
Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them.

notes: The Flocculation article (a frame candidate) was not crawled, so the entry is anchored on a section.

definition.text: The idea that soil aggregates form in levels, larger and less dense aggregates being built from smaller, denser ones.

facts.text: Primary particles join into sub-microaggregates and microaggregates below 250 μm and macroaggregates above 250 μm.

Organic binders are grouped as transient (polysaccharides), temporary (fungal hyphae and roots) and persistent (resistant aromatic compounds held by polyvalent cations, and strongly adsorbed polymers).
Temporary binders stabilize macroaggregates, while transient and persistent binders stabilize microaggregates.
Organic matter's role is hard to pin down: only part of it binds aggregates, beyond a threshold more adds no stability, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

conflicts.text: Macroaggregates are put above 2000 μm, mesoaggregates at 20-250 μm and microaggregates at 2-20 μm.
conflicts.note: Same page, Biological Factors section; the Factors section puts the macroaggregate limit at 250 μm.

conflicts.text: Microaggregates are given as 20-250 μm.
conflicts.note: Soil formation page; conflicts with the 2-20 μm microaggregate class above.

definition.text: Tests of how well soil aggregates survive stresses like those from water, wind or machinery, made at different aggregate size scales.

facts.text: Wet methods are usually more relevant because they mimic water erosion; dry methods suit arid regions, where wind erosion dominates.
Wet sieving slowly wets 2-4 mm aggregates, runs the sieve nest in a wet sieving apparatus at 30 rotations per minute for about 10 minutes, and reports a mean weight diameter.
The dry method sieves 0.92-1.68 mm aggregates in a rotary cylinder and reports the percentage of aggregates larger than 0.42 mm.
Slaking tests score how well aggregates hold together when submerged in water; one version uses a smartphone app in the field.

title: Slaking

definition.text: The process by which earth materials, such as soil aggregates, disintegrate and crumble when exposed to moisture.

facts.text: Water entering aggregates displaces air from their pores, and aggregates with trapped air burst: a direct mechanical destruction of structure by water.
Slaking rises with the rate of wetting: the faster the wetting, the more slaking occurs.
On sloping or bare ground slaking often leads to erosion; re-vegetating bare soil and limiting disturbance on slopes prevent it.
Slaking can affect the B horizon too, becoming a problem once the A horizon is disturbed or eroded; calcium replacing sodium reduces slaking in sodic soils.

notes: Article now crawled (Slaking (geology)); ground-cover and aggregate-stability sentences moved to mention_sent_ids.

title: Improving soil structure

definition.text: Practices that move soil toward a granular, crumb structure by raising its porosity, organic matter and microbial and faunal activity.

facts.text: Better structure means less erosion and overland flow, easier root access to water and nutrients, better seedling emergence through less crusting, and more infiltration and available water.
In cropping systems, wheat yields can rise by 10 kg/ha for every extra millimetre of rain able to infiltrate because of soil structure.
Adding mulch, manure or compost, practised since sedentary farming began, builds stable bridges between mineral particles.
Where warm, moist climates mineralize organic matter too fast, charcoal served instead, as in pre-Columbian terra preta; biochar is the modern version.
Liming increases porosity and aggregation because divalent calcium bridges negatively charged clay and organic molecules, and it also shields organic matter from mineralization.
Advised field practices include pasture phases in rotations, less tillage, not working soil when too wet or dry, and keeping ground cover against raindrop impact.
On irrigated sodic soils, gypsum is applied so calcium displaces sodium and lowers the exchangeable sodium percentage, and rapid wetting is avoided.
In irrigated horticulture, productivity under no-till or minimum tillage usually falls as structure degrades; the few exceptions are associated with high organic matter.

notes: Last fact sits uneasily with Soil aggregate stability's claim that reduced/zero tillage improves aggregation (S:7177c78b7e07); contexts differ (irrigated horticulture).

definition.text: A soil that loses its structure when wet and sets hard into a structureless mass as it dries.

facts.text: A hardsetting horizon dries to an almost uniform mass, with occasional cracks usually more than 0.1 m apart, too hard to push a forefinger into.
It is not permanently cemented: it softens when wet, and after flood irrigation or one intense rain it sets hard again on drying.
Such soils can be tilled only in a narrow moisture range, often leave a cloddy surface, restrict seedlings and roots, and shed rain as runoff.
Crusting soils are not necessarily hardsetting: a hardsetting horizon is thicker than a crust, in cultivated soils often as thick as the cultivated layer or more.

title: Loam

definition.text: Soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay.

facts.text: By weight a typical loam is about 40% sand, 40% silt and 20% clay, though the proportions vary.
In the USDA texture triangle, loam is the only class not dominated by sand, silt or clay.
Subtypes include sandy loam, silt loam, clay loam, sandy clay loam and silty clay loam, which drain water somewhat differently.
Loams hold more nutrients, water and humus than sandy soils, drain and aerate better than silty or clayey soils, and are easier to till than clays.
Loam is prized for farming and gardening because it keeps water and nutrients yet lets excess water drain away.
A soil dominated by one or two size groups can behave like loam if organic matter gives it strong granular structure; a textural loam loses its qualities when compacted or stripped of organic matter.
Most dictionaries, and many gardeners, define loam simply as soil containing humus, with no mention of particle size.

notes: Loam's use in building (rammed earth, adobe) was skipped as outside a soil science course.

title: Silt

definition.text: A granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, made mostly of broken quartz grains.

facts.text: Geologists define silt as detrital particles of 1/256 to 1/16 mm (about 4 to 63 microns); the USDA uses 0.05-0.002 mm.
The 63-micron upper limit is about the smallest grain the unaided eye can see; the 2-4 micron lower limit marks the change from quartz fragments to clay mineral particles.
Silt feels floury when dry, lacks plasticity when wet and feels gritty between the teeth, where clay-size particles feel smooth.
It forms by grinding of quartz grains, both in dust storms of very hot climates and by glaciers in very cold ones.
Wind-deposited silt forms loess, which makes up some of the most fertile farmland on Earth.
Silt's quartz grains supply no nutrients themselves but promote excellent soil structure, while smaller amounts of other silt-sized minerals provide nutrients.
Silt erodes easily, has poor mechanical properties and can liquefy in earthquakes; silt polluting water is called siltation.
The pipette method sizes silt by settling rate under Stokes' law: 60-micron grains settle through a metre of still water in five minutes, 2-micron grains take several days.

conflicts.text: Other geologists put silt at 2 to 63 microns (9 to 4 phi units).
conflicts.note: Lower limit 2 rather than about 4 microns.

conflicts.text: The International Society of Soil Science uses 0.02-0.002 mm.
conflicts.note: Upper limit 0.02 mm, against 0.05 mm (USDA) and about 63 microns (geology).

conflicts.text: ASTM sets silt between the No. 200 sieve and 0.005 mm.
conflicts.note: Lower limit 0.005 mm.

conflicts.text: US civil engineers call silt material passing a No. 200 sieve (0.074 mm or less) with little plasticity or cohesion.
conflicts.note: Upper limit 0.074 mm.

notes: Size limits are conventions of different bodies; S:d0dff564cea1 says the definitions agree well in practice, so not marked contested.

title: Sand

definition.text: A granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size: coarser than silt and finer than gravel.

facts.text: By the geologists' definition, sand grains range from 0.0625 mm (1/16 mm) to 2 mm in diameter.
As a soil textural class, sand is a soil with more than 85 percent sand-sized particles by mass.
In the United States sand has five grades, from very fine (1/16-1/8 mm) to very coarse (1-2 mm), based on the Krumbein phi scale.
Its commonest mineral inland and on non-tropical coasts is quartz, whose chemical inertness and hardness make it the commonest weathering-resistant mineral.
Calcium carbonate, such as aragonite made by coral and shellfish, is the second most common sand; gypsum sands are rarer.
Sand feels gritty when rubbed between the fingers.
Freshly weathered quartz sand is angular, while grains carried far by water or wind become rounded, so grains record their origin and transport.
Sandy soils drain very well and suit crops such as watermelons, peaches and peanuts; angular sharp sand is used to loosen clay soils.

conflicts.text: The Unified Soil Classification System defines sand as 0.074 to 4.75 mm.
conflicts.note: Engineering range tied to US standard sieves.

conflicts.text: A 1938 USDA specification set the smallest sand size at 0.05 mm.
conflicts.note: USDA lower limit versus 0.0625 mm in geology.

conflicts.text: Under Albert Atterberg's early 20th-century standard, particles as small as 0.02 mm counted as sand.
conflicts.note: Historical lower limit.

conflicts.text: A 1953 AASHTO engineering standard set the minimum sand size at 0.074 mm.
conflicts.note: Engineering lower limit.

notes: Construction-sand, resource and hazard material skipped as outside a soil science course.

title: Grain size

definition.text: The diameter of individual grains of sediment, or of the lithified particles in clastic rocks.

facts.text: Grain size differs from crystallite size, the size of a single crystal: one grain can contain several crystals.
Granular materials range from very small colloidal particles through clay, silt, sand, gravel and cobbles to boulders.
Size ranges set the limits of the named classes in the Udden-Wentworth scale used in the United States.
ISO 14688-1 classifies soils by size for engineering, from clay at 0.002 mm or less up to large boulders over 630 mm.
Grain-size data, with pore-size distribution and texture, are used to estimate hydraulic conductivity empirically, for example with Allen Hazen's formula.

notes: Dossier definition line is the sidebar title 'Granulometry'; the definition uses the real lead sentence S:ecd3bd943735.

definition.text: A logarithmic grain-size scale, created by W. C. Krumbein in 1934 from the Wentworth scale, that expresses size as minus the base-2 logarithm of diameter in millimetres.

facts.text: Sand spans phi -1 to 4 (2 mm to 62.5 μm), silt phi 4 to 8 (62.5 to 3.91 μm) and clay phi 8 to 10 (3.91 to 0.98 μm).
Above sand come granules (2-4 mm), then pebbles and cobbles, and boulders from 256 mm; some schemes call everything coarser than sand gravel.
The US sand grades divide at whole phi numbers between -1 and +4.
A reference diameter of 1 mm keeps the equation dimensionally consistent.

title: Sediment sorting

definition.text: The removal of a range of particle sizes from a sediment deposit by an agent such as a river or the wind.

facts.text: A sediment accumulation can be characterized by its grain size distribution.
Sorting is quantified by the Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation, calculated in phi units from percentiles of the grain size distribution such as the 84th.
Values below 0.35 mean very well sorted and values above 4.00 extremely poorly sorted, with well, moderately, poorly and very poorly sorted in between.
Wind is very effective at separating sand from silt and clay.

notes: The sorting formula sentence (S:5abec4a0e5cd) is garbled by extraction and was not cited.

title: Particle-size distribution

definition.text: A list of values or a mathematical function giving the relative amount, usually by mass, of particles of each size in a granular material.

facts.text: A soil's particle-size distribution is its texture, which governs properties such as hydraulic conductivity and water potential, though mineralogy can strongly modify them.
It affects the strength and load-bearing properties of rocks and soils.
Breaking soil into its particles takes significant energy; the resulting distribution is called a grain size distribution.
A distribution is usually defined by its measuring method; sieve analysis, the simplest, reports amounts in discrete size ranges between sieve sizes.
Results are given as a range analysis, listing the amount in each size range, or cumulatively, as the total retained or passed by a notional sieve.
Real particles are irregular, so how size is characterized depends heavily on the method of measurement.
Sedimentation methods size particles by their settling velocity in a liquid and suit sizes below 10 μm, but Brownian motion prevents reliable sub-micrometre measurement.
Laser diffraction infers size from the angle of scattered light, works best between 0.1 and 3,000 μm, and now dominates industrial measurement.

notes: Industrial dust-collection, nomenclature and Rosin-Rammler sections skipped as outside a soil science course.

title: Sieve analysis

definition.text: A procedure that measures the particle size distribution of a granular material by passing it through a stack of progressively finer sieves and weighing what each sieve holds.

facts.text: It works on almost any granular material, from sand, clay and soil to powders and seeds, and as the simplest sizing technique it is probably the most common.
A weighed sample goes into the top, coarsest sieve of a column; each lower sieve is finer, and a pan called the receiver sits at the base.
A mechanical shaker agitates the column for a set time; the material on each sieve is then weighed and divided by the total mass to give percent retained.
Dry sieving is accurate down to #100 mesh (150 μm) but much less so for finer material, as the energy needed and particle attraction rise with smaller sizes.
Wet sieving, with a water spray rinsing the stack until the outflow runs clear, handles suspensions and fine powders (mostly under 45 μm) that clump when dry.
The method assumes near-spherical particles, so elongated or flat grains give unreliable mass-based results.
For soils, silt and clay below 60 μm need a second sizing method, usually hydrometer or pipette, on the material from the bottom sieve.
In engineering, the soil's particle size distribution from sieving helps judge its mechanical properties and whether it can support a planned structure.

notes: Dossier cut the page after Methods > Throw-action; Limitations, Wet and Engineering applications facts come from the sentence index.

definition.text: A graph of the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size on a logarithmic scale.

facts.text: Percent retained on a sieve is its share of the total sample mass; adding each sieve's share to those above it gives the cumulative percent retained.
Cumulative percent passing equals 100% minus cumulative percent retained.
The curve's shape shows the gradation: a dense gradation gives an even curve, a uniform one a steep curve and a gap gradation a flat stretch in the medium sizes.
A soil's gradation is read from the grain size distribution curve produced by laboratory tests.

title: Atterberg limits

definition.text: A set of critical water contents (the shrinkage, plastic and liquid limits) that mark where a fine-grained soil changes from one state of consistency to another.

facts.text: Depending on how wet it is, a soil can be solid, semi-solid, plastic or liquid; each state behaves differently, so the boundaries are placed where the soil's behaviour changes.
A fine-grained soil's consistency varies with its water content, and because the transitions are gradual the standard tests define the boundaries by convention.
Albert Atterberg, a Swedish chemist and agronomist, devised the limits in 1911; Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them.
The limits separate silt from clay and different kinds of silts and clays; fine-grained soils are classified mainly by their Atterberg limits rather than by grain size.
The tests are used mostly on clayey and silty soils, because these interact with water, shrinking, swelling and changing in strength as their moisture varies.
The limits are closely related to compressibility, permeability and strength, and since they are simple to measure they serve for empirical estimates of those harder-to-measure properties.
Engineers run them early in design to check that a soil will have enough shear strength and will not change volume too much as it wets and dries.

notes: Flow index and toughness index subsections skipped as geotechnical detail. The dossier block stopped at 'Derived limits'; the derived-limit sentences were read with sqlite/ctx.

definition.text: The water content at which a clayey soil passes from behaving as a plastic solid to behaving as a liquid.

facts.text: The change to liquid behaviour is gradual, and soil at its liquid limit still has some strength: remolded soil there has an undrained shear strength of about 2 kPa.
In Casagrande's cup test, the liquid limit is the moisture content at which 25 drops of the cup close a groove cut in the soil over 12.7 mm.
The fall cone test instead measures how far a standard steel cone sinks into the soil; it is preferred in Europe because it depends less on the operator.
A liquid limit of 50 divides high-plasticity (H) from low-plasticity (L) fine soils in the USCS, and values over 50 suggest significant swelling.

definition.text: The water content below which a soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and becomes brittle, so it can no longer be rolled into a thin thread.

facts.text: It is found by rolling a thread of the soil's fine fraction on a flat, non-porous surface; as the soil dries, the thread starts breaking at larger diameters.
The plastic limit is the gravimetric moisture content at which the thread breaks apart at a diameter of 3.2 mm (about 1/8 inch).
A soil that cannot be rolled down to 3.2 mm at any moisture content is called non-plastic.
Remolded soil at the plastic limit is quite stiff, with an undrained shear strength of about 200 kPa.

conflicts.text: Soil mechanics defines the plastic limit using 3 mm diameter cylinders.
conflicts.note: Atterberg limits gives 3.2 mm (about 1/8 inch); the 3 mm figure may be a rounded value.

definition.text: The water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink.

facts.text: The shrinkage limit is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits.
Reported shrinkage limits differ by clay mineral: 8.5–15% for montmorillonite, 15–17% for illite and 25–29% for kaolinite.

definition.text: The span of water contents over which a soil behaves plastically, calculated as the liquid limit minus the plastic limit.

facts.text: Soils are described by plasticity index as non-plastic (0), slightly plastic (below 7), medium plastic (7–17) or highly plastic (above 17).
It indicates how much water the soil particles can absorb and correlates with permeability, compressibility and shear strength; highly plastic clays are less permeable and hard to compact.
A plasticity index above 35 signals high expansion potential in clay soils.
In the USCS, silts and clays are classified by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit on a plasticity chart.

title: Liquidity index

definition.text: An index that places a soil's natural water content on the scale between its plastic and liquid limits, LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL).

facts.text: The liquidity index expresses how water content affects the strength of saturated remolded soil.
At an index of 1 remolded soil sits at its liquid limit with an undrained shear strength of about 2 kPa; at 0 it is at the plastic limit, near 200 kPa.
The companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), is 0 at the liquid limit and 1 at the plastic limit, and turns negative when the soil is in the liquid state.
The liquidity and consistency indices always add up to 1.

notes: Covers the consistency index (Atterberg limits#Consistency index) as a fact rather than a separate entry.

definition.text: The ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is.

facts.text: Clay with an activity below 0.75 is termed inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal.
Clay minerals differ greatly in their limits: montmorillonite has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for illite and 30–110% for kaolinite.
In a table of example soils, a heavy clay with 72% clay had a liquid limit of 67 and a plasticity index of 40, while a well-graded loamy sand was non-plastic.

title: Shrink–swell capacity

definition.text: The degree to which certain clay minerals in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry.

facts.text: The capacity comes from clay minerals such as smectite, montmorillonite, vermiculite and illite, and the more of them a soil holds, the more severe its shrinking and swelling.
A soil with at least 5 percent of these minerals by weight may be able to shrink and swell.
It is measured as the coefficient of linear extensibility (COLE); a COLE above 0.06 can cause structural damage, and 0.06 means 100 inches of soil swell by 6 inches.
Among the soil separates, shrink/swell potential is very low for sand, low for silt and moderate to very high for clay.
Such soils fall in the Vertisol order: drying opens deep cracks that let water reach deeper layers, so shrinking and swelling repeat in cycles.
Contraction in dry spells can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracking also lets these soils recover quickly from compaction.
Swelling heaves structures and shrinking lets foundations settle unevenly; damage from shrink–swell clays is estimated at $7 billion a year.
Problems are worst where wet and dry seasons are sharply defined, and where pockets of wet soil sit beside dry soil and swell unevenly.

notes: Kept separate from Expansive clay: this entry is the property (mechanism, COLE, cycles, damage); Expansive clay is the material (lattice, identification, management).

title: Expansive clay

definition.text: A clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes.

facts.text: Clays are built of tetrahedral and octahedral sheets in 1:1 or 2:1 layers; expansive clays have an expanding 2:1 lattice, though some 2:1 clays do not expand.
In the laboratory, a plasticity index above 35 or liquid limit above 50, a free swell test comparing soil volume in water and kerosene, or X-ray detection of montmorillonite reveal expansive clay.
In the field, gilgai mounds and depressions, deep shrinkage cracks, or moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling indicate expansive soil.
Builders cope with deep foundations or piles, void spaces under slabs, chemical stabilizers such as lime, cement or fly ash, and steady moisture around structures.

conflicts.text: The Expansive clay lead groups kaolinite with the smectites as having the most dramatic shrink–swell capacity.
conflicts.note: Inconsistent with the page's own 2:1 expanding-lattice rule (S:296a8d21bb8e) and with Clay mineral, which classes kaolinite as a 1:1 clay (S:6d809205ff87); not used in the facts.

notes: Structural-engineering detail (void form materials, slab design) condensed into one fact.

title: Gilgai

definition.text: A microrelief of alternating mounds and depressions on the surface of shrink–swell clay soils.

facts.text: In Vertisols, repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves underlying material to the surface, creating gilgai.
Field surveys treat gilgai, along with deep shrinkage cracks, as a visible sign of expansive soil.

conflicts.text: USDA soil taxonomy's soil-order list calls the deep cracks that form in drying Vertisols gilgai.
conflicts.note: Expansive clay and Vertisol use gilgai for mound-and-depression microrelief, not for the cracks.

notes: No crawled Gilgai article; passes the 2+ pages test (Expansive clay, Vertisol, USDA soil taxonomy). May overlap a Vertisol-chapter entry.

title: Soil crust

definition.text: A surface layer of soil, often hardened and platy, that differs from the bulk soil beneath it.

facts.text: Crusts are biological when formed by communities of surface microorganisms, or physical when formed by impacts such as those of raindrops.
Physical crusts result from raindrop or trampling impact and are often harder than uncrusted soil because salts and silica accumulate in them.
Physical crusts often cut water infiltration, hinder plant establishment and, once broken up, erode quickly.
Low infiltration on bare ground is mostly due to a soil crust or surface seal.
Surface sealing lowers infiltration capacity, so in arid and semi-arid regions intense rain readily produces infiltration-excess overland flow.
Better soil structure means less surface crusting and so better seedling emergence.
Calcium exchanging for sodium reduces the particle dispersion, surface crusting and slaking typical of sodic soils.
Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent the breakdown of soil structure and the formation of crusts.

notes: Physical soil crusts are folded into this entry; biological crusts have their own section entry.

title: Biological soil crust

definition.text: A living community of organisms forming a crust on the soil surface in arid and semi-arid ecosystems.

facts.text: Cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses form these crusts even in deserts, capturing and storing a significant amount of carbon by photosynthesis.
The crusts fix carbon and nitrogen, stabilize soil, change surface albedo and water relations, and affect germination and nutrient levels of vascular plants.
Fire, recreation, grazing and other disturbance damage them, and recovering their composition and function can take a long time.
They are also called cryptogamic, microbiotic, microphytic or cryptobiotic soils, and can coexist with physical crusts while having a different ecological impact.

definition.text: The breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away.

facts.text: At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so particles repel one another when wet and aggregates disperse, whereas calcium and magnesium promote flocculation.
Dispersion is the opposite of flocculation; both are controlled mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content.
Dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure, clogs and seals surfaces where particles settle, and makes water turbid.
Dispersive layers usually lie in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate, so they may go unnoticed until disturbance exposes them to running water.
Dispersive soils are commoner in old landscapes, sodium collects low in the landscape, and dispersive subsoils feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure.
The key indicator is the exchangeable sodium percentage, sodium as a share of all cations: above 5% dispersion becomes possible, above 15% highly likely.
Management means avoiding disturbance, keeping vegetation cover, controlling salt, and adding gypsum where the soil has been disturbed.
Under irrigation, the decline of soil structure usually comes from aggregates breaking down and clay dispersing on rapid wetting.

title: Hydrophobic soil

definition.text: A soil whose particles repel water.

facts.text: It most often forms when fire or hot air drives waxy compounds out of the surface litter; these coat sandy particles in the upper soil, often beneath a layer of ash.

Sandy soils are most prone because large grains have little surface area and are easily coated, though coated silt or clay becomes severely repellent; it is reported on every continent except Antarctica.
Repellency slows infiltration, so runoff and erosion rise, wetting turns patchy and water escapes along preferential paths below the root zone; Australia has seen production losses of up to 80%.
Remedies include claying, adding clay such as calcium-bentonite, which raised one barley yield from 1.7 to 3.4 t/ha, and liming acidic soils to raise their pH.

notes: The 'Hydrophobic soil management' section (15 sentences) was missing from the dossier; read via sqlite.

definition.text: Tests that rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with the time one water drop takes to soak in.

facts.text: In the water drop penetration time test, soaking in under 5 seconds means not repellent, up to 1 minute slightly repellent, 1–10 minutes repellent, and over 10 minutes severely repellent.
A soil is judged hydrophobic when the contact angle between water and soil exceeds 90°.

The molarity of ethanol droplet test applies ethanol solutions of falling surface tension until one soaks in within 10 seconds; an index of 1 or less means non-repellent, 2.2 or more severely repellent.
Water entry pressure, linked to both the degree of repellency and pore size, is another indicator of infiltration.

definition.text: An engineering and geological system that classes soils by texture and grain size, giving each a two-letter symbol.

facts.text: It is the most common engineering soil classification in North America and can be applied to most unconsolidated materials.
Letters name the main material (G gravel, S sand, M silt, C clay, O organic, PT peat), and a second letter gives grading (W or P) or liquid limit (H high, L low).
Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained soils such as sands and gravels, fine-grained soils such as silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat.
A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% is retained on the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve; the No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel.
Sands and gravels are divided by grain size and grading, while silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils.
With 5–12% fines, both grading and plasticity matter and a dual symbol may be used, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt.
Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm.
The European system, ISO 14688, is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

conflicts.text: The USCS lead table glosses W (well-graded) as many particles of about the same size and P (poorly graded) as many different sizes.
conflicts.note: Reversed relative to Soil gradation (S:5c50677c4d23) and Soil mechanics (S:43c862203d3f), which define well-graded as a wide range of sizes; the gloss is not used in the facts.

conflicts.text: Gravel gives the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' number 4 mesh spacing as 4.76 mm.
conflicts.note: USCS sources give the No. 4 sieve opening as 4.75 mm.

title: USCS coarse-grained soil groups
article: Soil mechanics#Classification of sands and gravels

definition.text: The USCS groups for soils with more than half their weight retained on the No. 200 sieve: gravels (G) and sands (S), subdivided by grading and fines content.

facts.text: A coarse soil is gravel if more than 50% of its coarse fraction stays on the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve, and sand if at least 50% of it passes.
Clean gravels and sands, with under 5% fines, are well graded (GW, SW) or poorly graded (GP, SP); GW needs Cu ≥ 4 and SW Cu ≥ 6, both with 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3.
With more than 12% fines they become silty (GM, SM) or clayey (GC, SC), according to whether the fines classify as silt or clay.
A well-graded soil has a wide range of particle sizes; sands and gravels with 5–12% fines get dual symbols such as SW-SC.

notes: Anchored on the Soil mechanics section devoted to it; criteria come from the USCS ASTM D-2487 table.

title: USCS fine-grained soil groups
article: Soil mechanics#Classification of silts and clays

definition.text: The USCS groups for soils with 50% or more passing the No. 200 sieve, classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit.

facts.text: On the plasticity chart the A-line separates clays (C) from silts (M), and a liquid limit of 50% separates high-plasticity (H) from low-plasticity (L) soils.
The inorganic groups are lean clay (CL), silt (ML), fat clay (CH) and elastic silt (MH); CL needs a plasticity index above 7 and ML one below 4.
Organic silts and clays (OL, OH) are told apart from inorganic ones by how their plasticity and liquid limit change on oven drying; highly organic soils are peat (PT).
Soils whose limits plot in the hatched zone near the chart's origin get the dual symbol CL-ML.

notes: Image: the USCS plasticity chart with the A-line.

title: Tilth

definition.text: The physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop.

facts.text: Tilth depends on how well soil particles form stable aggregates, on moisture, aeration and soil life, and on rates of infiltration and drainage, and it can change quickly.
Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water; roots grow only where tilth allows enough oxygen, and such soil holds a reasonable store of water and nutrients.
Good tilth balances aggregate tensile strength against friability, so aggregates break readily under shallow tilling; high tensile strength gives large cemented clods.
Well-aggregated soil has a range of pore sizes: large pores drain fast and keep air moving in wet periods, while small pores hold water through dry spells.
Tillage aims to improve tilth, but the aggregation it creates is short-lived, and long-term ploughing tends to break down the soil carbon sponge and compact the soil.
In 2021 the soil volume tilled worldwide was estimated at 1840 km3 a year, against 960 km3 a year moved naturally by plant roots and earthworms.
The most stable tilth comes from roots, microbes and earthworms: root exudates feed bacteria that secrete polysaccharides and fungi whose hyphae bind particles into aggregates.
Crop rotations with grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild tilth in compacted soils.

title: Physical properties of soil

definition.text: The measurable physical traits of a soil, which in falling order of importance for crops are texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, colour and resistivity.

facts.text: These properties change with depth through the soil horizons, and most of them govern aeration and how well water enters and is held in the soil.
Texture comes from the proportions of sand, silt and clay; at the next scale up, coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind these separates into peds.
Bulk density measured at a standard moisture estimates compaction, and porosity is the part of the soil volume filled by gases or water.
Sand holds little water but drains fast and is well aerated; clay holds much water but drains very slowly and is poorly aerated; silt lies in between.
Clay stores plant nutrients well and resists pH change, while sand does both poorly and has a high potential for pollutant leaching.
Sandy soils warm quickly in spring and resist compaction; clay soils warm slowly and compact easily.
Silt is highly susceptible to both wind and water erosion, whereas clay resists water erosion when it is aggregated.

notes: Hub page. Structure, Density, Porosity, Temperature and Colour sections were left to the chapters that own Soil structure, Bulk density / Pore space in soil, soil temperature and Soil color; none of those sections appeared in the dossier.

definition.text: The ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture.

facts.text: Consistency is assessed air-dry, moist and wet, and in those states it depends on clay content.
Dry soil is rubbed to test its resistance to crumbling, moist soil is pressed between thumb and finger, and wet soil is judged for stickiness and plasticity.
Standard terms run from loose to extremely hard when dry, loose to extremely firm when moist, and nonsticky to very sticky and nonplastic to very plastic when wet.
Cemented consistency, from calcium carbonate, silica, oxides or salts, hardly changes with moisture and ranges from weakly cemented to indurated, which needs hammer blows to break.
The measures are close to subjective, because they rely on how the soil feels in each state.
Consistency roughly predicts cultivation problems and a soil's ability to support buildings and roads, though more precise strength tests usually precede construction.
It is one of the traits used to describe soil horizons and to group soils into series and families.

definition.text: A measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of an electric current.

facts.text: Resistivity affects how fast buried metal and concrete structures corrode.
Wetter soil or a higher electrolyte concentration lowers resistivity, raising conductivity and the rate of corrosion.
Values typically range from about 1 to 100000 Ω·m, the extremes being saline soils and dry soils over crystalline rocks.

title: Specific surface area

definition.text: The surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as surface area per unit mass.

facts.text: Specific surface area, together with the particles' unbalanced electric charges, sets their role in soil fertility as measured by cation exchange capacity.
Sand has the least specific surface area and is least active, silt is intermediate, and clay is the most active.
Clay minerals form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram.
Clay's very high specific surface area and many negative charges give soil its high capacity to retain water and nutrients.
The water a soil holds at field capacity depends on the specific surface area of its particles.
Particles of one textural class share properties tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as cation exchange capacity.

conflicts.text: Physical properties of soil describes specific surface area as the surface-area-to-volume ratio of soil particles.
conflicts.note: Soil mechanics defines it per unit mass (S:c2691e02484c), which the definition uses.

notes: No crawled article; mentioned on Physical properties of soil, Soil mechanics, Soil, Soil moisture, Soil texture and Clay. Drafted here because the richest sentences are on Physical properties of soil; check against chunk 05 (Soil texture, Clay) for overlap.

title: Gravel

definition.text: A loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand.

facts.text: Definitions vary: many geologists use loose rounded particles over 2 mm, the USDA and Soil Science Society of America use 2–80 mm, and the Udden-Wentworth scale 2–64 mm.
In soil texture analysis, fragments larger than 2.0 mm are removed before the textural class is set but still appear in the name, as in gravelly sandy loam.
Most gravel comes from weathering bedrock; quartz is its commonest mineral because it is hard and inert, and river transport rounds the fragments quickly.
Natural gravel conducts water fast, sometimes above 1 cm/s, so gravel deposits make aquifers, while gravelly soils hold little moisture or nutrients and carry sparse plant life.

notes: Size limits differ by system (USDA, Udden-Wentworth, ISO 14688, USACE, German); treated as definitional differences, not conflicts. Construction and commercial detail skipped.

definition.text: The twelve named categories into which the USDA groups soils by their percentages of sand, silt and clay.

facts.text: The twelve classes are sand, loamy sand, sandy loam, loam, silt loam, silt, sandy clay loam, clay loam, silty clay loam, sandy clay, silty clay and clay.
A class is named after its main particle size or a mix of the most abundant sizes, as in "sandy clay" or "silty clay".
"Loam" describes a soil with roughly equal properties of sand, silt and clay, and it combines into further class names such as "clay loam" and "silt loam".
The USDA and WRB systems both use 12 textural classes, while the UK-ADAS system uses 11.
Texture classes help judge which crops suit a soil and predict its response to drought or its lime (calcium) needs.

definition.text: A triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay, used to read off a soil's texture class.

facts.text: One side of the triangle shows percent sand, another percent clay and the third percent silt.
Once a sample's sand, clay and silt percentages are known, the triangle assigns its texture class; the reading works starting from any side.
For example, a soil with 70 percent sand and 10 percent clay plots as a sandy loam.
On the USDA triangle, loam is the only class in which none of sand, silt or clay predominates.
Used in reverse, the triangle gives a rough estimate of sand, silt and clay percentages for a soil classed by feel.
It is a ternary plot: three variables that sum to a constant, usually 100%, so knowing two fixes the third and all three fit on one flat triangle.
Each component is 100% at one corner and 0% along the opposite edge; grid lines parallel to the edges make values easy to read.
For example, a sample with 50% clay and 20% silt must contain 30% sand for the three to total 100%.

definition.text: Set ranges of particle size, sand, silt and clay, into which a soil's mineral particles are sorted.

facts.text: Texture considers only particles smaller than two millimetres across: sand, silt and clay.
In the USDA scheme, clay particles are under 0.002 mm, silt runs from 0.002 to 0.05 mm, and sand is larger than 0.05 mm.
USDA sand is split into five grades, from very fine sand (0.05–0.10 mm) through fine, medium and coarse to very coarse sand (1.00–2.00 mm).
Other systems draw different limits; the WRB, for instance, puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm instead of 0.05 mm.
Clay particles are plate-shaped rather than spherical, which gives them a larger specific surface area.
Sand is the least active separate, with the least specific surface area, silt comes next, and clay is the most active.
Water-holding capacity is low in sand, medium to high in silt and high in clay, while drainage is respectively high, slow to medium, and very slow.

conflicts.text: Atterberg's international system set the upper limit of silt at 20 μm.
conflicts.note: Older international scheme; the USDA puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.05 mm.

conflicts.text: The WRB puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm.
conflicts.note: System difference, not an error; the USDA uses 0.05 mm.

definition.text: The first soil particle-size classification, proposed by Albert Atterberg in 1905 from his studies in southern Sweden.

facts.text: Atterberg set silt's upper limit at 20 μm: finer particles are invisible to the eye, coagulate with salts, show the fastest 24-hour capillary rise, and leave pores too small for root hairs.
Commission One of the International Society of Soil Science recommended the system at the First International Congress of Soil Science, held in Washington in 1927.
Australia adopted the system, whose equal logarithmic size intervals are seen as an attractive feature worth keeping.
The USDA adopted its own system in 1938, and the FAO used the USDA system for the FAO-UNESCO world soil map and recommended it.

definition.text: A qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand.

facts.text: A ball of soil is pushed between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon that extends over the finger until it breaks under its own weight.
The unbroken length of the ribbon helps indicate how much clay the sample holds.
Rubbing a wetted pinch in the palm shows the sand content: sandy soils feel gritty, silty soils smooth and clayey soils sticky.
It gives no exact sand, silt and clay values, but a trained person following its flowchart can judge their relative proportions accurately.
Needing little or no equipment, it allows quick, frequent checks that reveal variation within and between fields and boundaries between soil map units.
The method takes practice, and the WRB offers its own alternative texture-by-feel flowchart.

definition.text: A laboratory sedimentation test that estimates a soil's percent sand, silt and clay from how fast dispersed particles settle, based on Stokes' law.

facts.text: Stokes' law links a particle's settling velocity to its size, so suspended particles separate by size as they sink.
The soil is shaken overnight with sodium hexametaphosphate, a dispersing agent that breaks up aggregates, then made up with water in a one-litre cylinder.
After mixing, sand (over 50 microns) settles first and silt next, while clay (2 microns or finer) stays above the silt layer.
An ASTM 152H hydrometer reads grams of suspended material per litre: at 40 seconds for silt plus clay, giving sand, and after 6–8 hours for the clay still suspended.
Percent silt is 100 minus the sum of percent clay and percent sand; subtracting a blank reading removes the need for temperature correction.
Introduced in 1927, the method is still widely used, but flaws found in the empirical 1927 protocol mean its original procedure and settling cylinder should not be used.
Platy clay particles settle broadside with extra drag, so they are sized too small and the fine fraction is overestimated; below 0.2 micron, Brownian motion stops particles settling by Stokes' law.
Sieving cannot size silt and clay on its own, so sedimentation analysis, such as the hydrometer or pipette method, covers the fine end of the size distribution.

title: Laser diffraction particle sizing

definition.text: An optical method that measures particle-size distribution from the way particles, dispersed in a liquid or as dry powder, bend light.

facts.text: The diffraction angle depends on particle size, so the pattern records the mix of sizes; it is analysed with Mie or Fraunhofer theory, Fraunhofer often being recommended for natural soils.
Fraunhofer theory treats only diffraction at the particle's edge and needs no optical data; Mie theory adds refraction, reflection and absorption but needs the material's complex refractive index.
The smaller the particle, the larger the scattering angle; with Mie theory the lower detection limit is thought to be around 10 nm.
Results are volume-weighted equivalent spherical diameters, summarised as the median D50, the D10 and D90, and the span, (D90 – D10)/D50.
It is fast and cost-effective, handles very small samples such as forensic ones, and built-in dispersion lets dry samples skip the preparation that sieving and sedimentation require.
With samples well dispersed, one technique covers the whole size range, including silt and clay, with no need to combine two methods.
Both theories assume spherical particles, so platy clay is sized by its plate cross-section and usually measured larger than by sedimentation analysis.
Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method it is fast, reproducible and needs small samples, and it gave better precision.

notes: Article moved from Soil texture#Laser Diffraction to the full Laser diffraction analysis page; the four original facts cite the Soil texture section.

definition.text: A hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption.

facts.text: Particle size is calculated from terminal settling velocities using Stokes' law.
The absorption of X-rays, interpreted with the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class.
It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, particulate organic matter (POM) and rapid methods.

definition.text: Clay's capacity, when wet, to be moulded into a shape that it then keeps, its defining mechanical property.

facts.text: Plasticity comes from clay minerals, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist, giving clay its cohesion.
In kaolinite, a film of water molecules hydrogen-bonds the plates: weak enough to let them slip during moulding, strong enough to hold the new shape.
Drying removes most of the water so the plates bond directly, leaving clay rigid but fragile; moistened again, it becomes plastic once more.
Clay stays plastic across a range of water contents, from the plastic limit, just moist enough to mould, to the liquid limit, just dry enough to hold its shape.
For kaolinite clay, the plastic limit is about 36% to 40% and the liquid limit about 58% to 72%.
Soils, particularly clays, deform inelastically under load, mainly through rearrangement of clusters of neighbouring grains, in ways that depend on microstructure, chemistry and water content.

definition.text: The difference between clay as a class of very fine particle sizes and clay as material made of clay minerals, two overlapping but distinct definitions.

facts.text: Clays differ from other fine-grained soils in size and mineralogy; silts contain no clay minerals and tend to be coarser than clays.
The silt–clay boundary depends on the discipline: usually 2 μm for geologists and soil scientists, often 4–5 μm for sedimentologists, and 1 μm for colloid chemists; ISO 14688 uses 2 μm.
Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity, measured with the Atterberg limits, rather than by size.

Size does not fix mineral makeup: textural clay may be very fine quartz or layered secondary minerals, so a size class shares surface-area properties but not chemistry-linked ones such as cation exchange.

conflicts.text: Sedimentologists often place the silt–clay boundary at 4–5 μm and colloid chemists at 1 μm.
conflicts.note: Discipline convention; soil scientists and ISO 14688 use 2 μm.

conflicts.text: The sediment grain-size scale puts clay below 3.9 μm.
conflicts.note: Sedimentological scale; soil science uses 2 μm (0.002 mm).

definition.text: How a high clay content shapes a soil's value for farming, trading poor drainage against greater fertility.

facts.text: Clay is often seen as undesirable for farming, although some clay is a necessary part of good soil.
Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before they suit crops.
Their higher cation-exchange capacity makes them more fertile and better at holding nutrients, keeping more land in production rather than fallow.
Clay soils resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils because their particles bond tightly to each other.

definition.text: An engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil according to the range of particle sizes it contains.

facts.text: Gravels and sands are well graded, with a good spread of sizes from the No. 4 to No. 200 sieves, or poorly graded, which divides into uniformly graded and gap-graded soils.
Fine-grained soils, mainly silts and clays, are classed by their Atterberg limits instead.
Gradation is read from a grain-size distribution curve built from sieve or hydrometer analysis, following either the USCS or the AASHTO system.
It signals compressibility, shear strength and hydraulic conductivity: poorly graded soils drain better through more voids and liquefy more easily, while well-graded soils compact further.

title: Coefficients of uniformity and curvature
article: Soil gradation#Calculating the coefficients of uniformity and curvature

definition.text: Two values, Cu and Cc, calculated from grain diameters on a soil's size-distribution curve and compared with published limits to grade a coarse soil.

facts.text: Cu, a crude shape parameter, is calculated from D60 and D10, the grain diameters at which 60% and 10% of the sample passes.
Cc, a shape parameter, combines D30, D10 and D60, the grain diameters at 30%, 10% and 60% passing.
Under the USCS, a gravel is well graded (GW) when Cu > 4 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (GP).
A sand is well graded (SW) when Cu ≥ 6 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (SP).

title: Mud

definition.text: Loam, silt or clay mixed with water.

facts.text: Mud usually forms after rainfall or near sources of water.
On the sediment grain-size scale, mud covers silt (3.9–62.5 μm) and clay (below 3.9 μm).
Over geological time, ancient mud deposits hardened into sedimentary rocks such as shale and mudstone.
Mixed with water, set in moulds and dried in the open air, mud makes mudbricks, or adobe, long used for building houses.

definition.text: A science on the border of agronomy and physics that studies agroecosystems with the methods of the physical sciences.

facts.text: It is close to biophysics but restricted to the physics of the plants, animals, soil and atmosphere involved in farming.
It grew out of soil physics and first studied relations within the soil, then widened to crop properties and the quality and safety of food and raw farm produce.
Research centres include the Institute of Agrophysics of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Lublin and the Agrophysical Research Institute in St. Petersburg.
Soil science lists agrophysics among its related disciplines.

title: Friability

definition.text: The tendency of a solid material to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing.

facts.text: The opposite of friable is indurate; geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together.
Good tilth balances aggregate tensile strength against friability; high tensile strength gives large cemented clods of low friability.
Soil profile descriptions record it: the Cecil soil's surface horizon is described as a very friable sandy loam.
Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils in Waikato to improve their drainage and friability for growing kūmara and taro.

notes: General materials-science page; facts drawn from its definition and geology lines plus soil sentences on other pages.

definition.text: A law giving the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers.

facts.text: George Gabriel Stokes derived it in 1851 from the Navier–Stokes equations in the limit of small Reynolds numbers.
It assumes laminar flow, no inertia, and smooth, uniform, spherical particles that do not interfere with each other.
To stay within 10% error, velocities must be limited to those giving a Reynolds number below 1.
A settling particle reaches terminal velocity when drag plus buoyancy balance its weight: v = (2/9)(ρp − ρf)gR²/μ.
Because the excess weight grows with R³ and the drag only with R, settling velocity grows with R² and so varies greatly with particle size.
It explains the sedimentation of small particles in water, and why cloud droplets stay aloft until they grow to a critical size.
Hydrometer analysis of fine soils rests on it: a grain's diameter is calculated from how far it falls in a known time.
The pipette method also uses Stokes settling to measure coarse and fine silt in a sediment sample.

title: Particle size analysis

definition.text: The collective name for laboratory techniques that measure the size range or mean size of particles in a powder or liquid sample.

facts.text: Methods use light, ultrasound, electric fields, gravity or centrifugation, and most infer size from another measurement rather than measuring diameters directly.
Irregular particles are sized as an equivalent sphere: sieving gives a volume-based diameter, optical methods an area-based one.
Different methods are not expected to give identical results, so the method should match the use the data will be put to.
Sieving has long been the choice for soil texture, but laser diffraction is increasingly used because it is faster and highly reproducible.

notes: Also cites Particle size (Expressions for sphere size); that general page adds no separate soil entry.

title: Pipette method

definition.text: A laboratory sedimentation method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample from settling rates given by Stokes' law.

facts.text: Like the hydrometer, it is a sedimentation analysis widely used in soil engineering and geology to classify sediments.
It sizes the silt and clay finer than 60 μm that pass the bottom sieve of a sieve analysis.
Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method, laser diffraction analysis gave better precision.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; mentioned on Silt, Soil texture, Sieve analysis and Laser diffraction analysis.

title: Clod

definition.text: A mass of soil formed artificially by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, as opposed to a naturally formed ped.

facts.text: Clods result from tillage, excavation and heavy machinery used on wet soil; compaction gives hard clods instead of soft peds.
Tilling wetter or drier than the optimum water content produces large clods, and hardsetting soils give a cloddy surface when tilled.
Harrowing breaks up clods to create a tilth suitable for sowing.
Clods of 2 to 100 mm make up the second of the four classes of soil-surface roughness.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; defined on Ped, Aggregate (geology) and Physical properties of soil.
